raw_case_text:
Our patient was a relatively healthy 59-year-old African-American male who presented with several weeks of pruritus, jaundice, nausea, and weight loss. His past medical history was significant for hypertension and he did not consume alcohol, IV drugs, or herbal supplements. Physical findings included jaundice, without signs of chronic liver disease, and a benign abdomen without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Labs showed elevated liver enzymes in an obstructive pattern (Figure 1).
He underwent extensive testing for infectious causes which was negative, including hepatitis A, B, C, E, leptospirosis, VDRL, and peripheral smear performed for malaria. Further evaluation including ANA, Smooth muscle antibody, Antimitochondrial antibodies, IgG elevated antibodies, alpha-1 antitrypsin, and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 were all negative. Ultrasound showed only hepatic steatosis, though further abdominal CT showed an enlarged celiac axis lymph node (>1 cm) and portal lymphadenopathy. There was no duct dilatation or either intrahepatic or extrahepatic ducts on endoscopic ultrasound. Cytology from the enlarged celiac node showed small lymphocytes, not diagnostic for lymphoma. An ultrasound-guided liver biopsy was therefore performed (Figure 2).
This showed noncaseating granulomas and bile duct damage, highly suggestive of sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis was further confirmed with high activity of angiotensin-converting enzyme and mediastinal/hilar lymphadenopathy in CT of the chest. The patient was started on budesonide and 6-mercaptopurine therapy with marked improvement of symptoms. Repeat labs showed resolution of ACE inhibitor levels and liver chemistries except ALP (Figure 1). He underwent spirometry which showed a mild reduction in FEV1/FVC (66%). After approximately 8 months of being asymptomatic on treatment, he was seen in the emergency room for complaints of yellowing of skin, itching, pale stools, and weight loss, reportedly going on for the past 6 months. Laboratory findings showed worsening hepatic function with severe direct hyperbilirubinemia. He was started on methylprednisolone for a suspected sarcoidosis flare-up, with no improvement. He underwent an abdominal ultrasound which showed a dilated common bile duct measuring 1.6 cm and biliary sludge, which was not present before. Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography revealed persistently enlarged perihepatic and periportal lymph nodes and a mass in the ampulla of the pancreas (Figure 3).
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography showed a biliary stricture and a double-duct sign (proximal pancreatic and common bile duct dilation) with biliary stricture biopsy displaying a cluster of atypical glandular cells, likely adenocarcinoma (Figures 4 and 5). Workup for malignancy included CT PET showing multiple hepatic lesions, the largest measuring 1.3 cm along with other known lymphadenopathy and pancreatic mass. Staging diagnostic laparoscopy showed no evidence of carcinomatosis during which a wedge liver biopsy was taken which showed granulomatous hepatitis, but keratin cocktail immunohistochemistry was negative for carcinoma. He underwent a pancreaticoduodenectomy and antrectomy with no complications.
The pancreatic mass biopsy confirmed pancreatobiliary origin of carcinoma. Three out of 28 lymph nodes were positive for malignant cells and showed evidence of sarcoidosis. The final staging was pT3b pN1, stage 3A. Immunohistochemistry studies revealed a mismatch repair proteins expressed, MSS. He was started on adjuvant chemotherapy and pancreatic enzyme replacement.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old African American man presented with several weeks of pruritus, jaundice, nausea, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with several weeks of progressive cholestatic jaundice, generalized pruritus, nausea, and weight loss. After an initial diagnosis of hepatic sarcoidosis and 8 months of clinical remission on immunosuppressive therapy, he represented to the emergency department with a 6-month recurrence of worsening jaundice, pruritus, acholic (pale) stools, and weight loss unresponsive to methylprednisolone.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of hypertension; denied alcohol consumption, intravenous drug use, or herbal supplement intake.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for jaundice, pruritus, nausea, pale stools, and weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination demonstrated cutaneous and scleral jaundice without stigmata of chronic liver disease, abdominal tenderness, hepatosplenomegaly, or ascites.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed an obstructive cholestatic liver enzyme elevation and elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) activity. Infectious panels (hepatitis A, B, C, and E, leptospirosis, VDRL, and peripheral blood smear for malaria), autoimmune markers (ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, serum IgG), alpha-1 antitrypsin, and baseline CA 19-9 were all negative/normal. Initial abdominal ultrasound showed only hepatic steatosis; spirometry showed mild airflow obstruction (FEV1/FVC 66%). At representation 8 months later, labs showed severe direct hyperbilirubinemia, and repeat abdominal ultrasound revealed a newly dilated common bile duct (1.6 cm) with biliary sludge.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial abdominal CT showed enlarged celiac axis (>1 cm) and portal lymph nodes; chest CT showed mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy; endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) with fine-needle aspiration of the celiac node showed benign small lymphocytes without biliary duct dilation. Initial ultrasound-guided liver biopsy demonstrated noncaseating granulomas and bile duct injury. Upon representation 8 months later, MRCP identified a mass in the ampulla/head of the pancreas with persistent perihepatic/periportal lymphadenopathy; ERCP demonstrated a distal biliary stricture and a double-duct sign, with brush/biopsy cytology showing atypical glandular cells suspicious for adenocarcinoma. Staging PET-CT showed the pancreatic head mass, lymphadenopathy, and hepatic lesions up to 1.3 cm; staging laparoscopy with wedge liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis (negative for carcinoma on keratin IHC). Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple resection) pathology confirmed stage IIIA (pT3b pN1, mismatch repair-proficient/MSS) pancreatobiliary adenocarcinoma with 3 of 28 lymph nodes positive for both metastatic adenocarcinoma and noncaseating sarcoid granulomas.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed stage IIIA (pT3b pN1) pancreatobiliary adenocarcinoma coexisting with systemic and hepatic sarcoidosis; leptospirosis, viral hepatitides, and primary biliary/autoimmune cholangiopathies were excluded. Initially treated for hepatic sarcoidosis with oral budesonide and 6-mercaptopurine with 8 months of biochemical and clinical remission. Following representation with malignant biliary obstruction and failure of empiric methylprednisolone, he underwent uncomplicated Whipple pancreaticoduodenectomy with antrectomy and was initiated on adjuvant chemotherapy and pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy.
